broccoli-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Broccoli, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is an edible flower head of Brassica oleracea var. italica, a relative of cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts. Fresh broccoli is usually steamed, boiled or roasted without added fat, preserving most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli contains more vitamin C than an orange.
In ancient Rome broccoli was called “little tree”.
There are over 100 varieties, including green, purple and Roman broccoli.
Broccoli is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
In Japan broccoli is often served as a salad with soy sauce and sesame seeds.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: One hundred grams of broccoli provides about 90 mg of vitamin C, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Rich in phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Broccoli has only about 35 kcal per 100 g, making it an excellent choice for weight management.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin K may affect the efficacy of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Broccoli can be eaten raw in salads, steamed, boiled for 3–5 minutes, or roasted with herbs. When cooking without added fat, a steamer or microwave is recommended.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh broccoli in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Use within 3–5 days. For freezing, blanch for 2–3 minutes, cool quickly and pack in airtight bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit smoothie is a beverage made from whole fruits without any dairy ingredients. It retains most of the fiber, vitamins, and minerals found in fresh fruit and is suitable for those avoiding dairy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Smoothies made with whole fruit retain more fiber than juice made from the same amount of fruit.
The absence of dairy makes it suitable for vegans and people with lactose intolerance.
A wide variety of fruits allows easy flavor changes and nutritional tweaks.
Combining different fruits can provide a broader spectrum of antioxidants than a single‑fruit blend.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fruit smoothies provide vitamin C, vitamin A, folate, and other micronutrients that support immunity and skin health.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Whole fruits keep dietary fiber intact, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Without dairy, the drink is low‑calorie and contains minimal saturated fat.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids from the fruit help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content of fresh fruit contributes to overall fluid balance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even though natural, fruit smoothies can be high in fructose, which should be considered by people with diabetes or those monitoring weight.

items.title: Allergies
items.content: Certain fruits (e.g., kiwi, mango) may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Microbial growth
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the smoothie can become a breeding ground for bacteria. Consume immediately or refrigerate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the smoothie on its own, use it as a base for breakfast bowls, add to oatmeal, plant‑based yogurt, or incorporate into dessert recipes. Optional add‑ins include chia seeds, nuts, or protein powder.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared smoothie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized containers.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried ice cream is a dessert consisting of a frozen ice‑cream ball coated in a crumb mixture (often cookies, cornflakes or panko) and quickly deep‑fried in hot oil. The interior stays cold and creamy while the exterior becomes crisp and lightly caramelized.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried ice cream originated in Asian cuisine and is especially popular in Thailand, China and Japan.
The ice‑cream ball is typically frozen to –30 °C to withstand the brief frying without melting.
High‑smoke‑point oils such as peanut or canola are commonly used for frying.
The coating can be flavored with coconut, cocoa, spices or dried fruit.
Many restaurants serve it with chocolate, caramel or fruit sauces.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: As a dairy product, fried ice cream provides calcium important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The milk base supplies vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Dairy protein contributes to tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Psychological pleasure
items.content: The contrast of a hot crunchy shell and a cold creamy core enhances sensory enjoyment.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: Fried ice cream can be calorie‑dense; people watching weight or blood‑sugar levels should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose non‑dairy alternatives.

items.title: Trans fats in frying oil
items.content: Repeated use of oil can generate trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Burn hazard
items.content: Hot oil can cause burns; preparation and serving should be done carefully.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried ice cream immediately after cooking while the crust is still warm. Sprinkle with powdered sugar, toasted coconut, nuts, or drizzle with chocolate, caramel, or berry sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fried ice cream is best enjoyed right away. If leftovers are needed, keep the frozen balls in a sealed container at –18 °C. Before refrying, fully thaw them.

content.title: About
content.content: A coated pork chop is a tender piece of pork covered with breadcrumbs or a seasoned coating and fried or baked until golden. The product is sold ready‑to‑cook without added salt, allowing you to control sodium intake during preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The coating helps retain juices, keeping the meat moist.
Coated chops are popular for quick meals because they cook fast on a skillet or in the oven.
No‑salt versions are suitable for people monitoring their sodium consumption.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12, zinc, and iron.
Traditional breading is made from breadcrumbs, often flavored with herbs and spices.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coated chops supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Zinc and iron in pork support immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Moisture retention
items.content: The breading reduces moisture loss during cooking, resulting in a juicier product.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: Ready‑to‑cook format saves time and makes it easy to prepare a nutritious meal.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Coated pork chops can contain a notable amount of saturated fat, which should be considered in low‑fat diets.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The tasty crust can lead to larger portions than intended.

items.title: Allergy to breading
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to wheat or other ingredients in the coating.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coated pork chops can be pan‑fried with a little oil, baked at 200 °C for 15‑20 minutes, or grilled. Lightly season with salt and your favorite spices before cooking for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Discard any pieces with off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese potato hash brown is a golden‑fried patty made from grated potatoes mixed with shredded cheese and seasonings. It is commonly served in fast‑food restaurants as a quick side dish or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hash browns originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover potatoes.
Cheese not only adds flavor but also helps bind the mixture, making the patty crispier.
Different countries use various cheeses: cheddar, mozzarella, gouda, etc.
Hash browns are often served with ranch dressing or sour cream.
Fast preparation (about 10‑15 minutes) makes them popular in chain restaurants.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamins B6 and B9, important for metabolism.

items.title: Protein from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds dairy protein that aids tissue repair.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The carbohydrate content provides a quick source of energy, convenient for fast‑food settings.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese contains saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt is often added for taste; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hash browns hot, often with a dipping sauce such as ketchup, mayo, or ranch, or with sour cream. They can be added to burgers, salads, or enjoyed alone as a snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hash browns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: A diet carbonated beverage with chocolate cola flavor combines the classic cola taste with a subtle hint of cocoa, while containing no sugar. It is designed for those who want a sweet flavor without extra calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate cola flavor first appeared in the early 2000s as a limited‑edition experiment.
Diet colas typically use artificial sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose.
Caffeine content in diet colas is usually 30–40 mg per 330 ml, comparable to regular cola.
The chocolate note is achieved with natural or artificial cocoa flavorings.
The drink is often marketed as “sugar‑free but flavorful” in advertising campaigns.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Absence of sugar reduces the calorie count to about 1–2 kcal per 100 ml, making it suitable for weight control.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Caffeine can increase alertness and improve concentration, though the amount is moderate.

items.title: Sugar‑free
items.content: Lack of glucose and fructose is beneficial for people with diabetes, provided they are not sensitive to artificial sweeteners.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any carbonated drink, it contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Some versions are fortified with B3 and B6 vitamins, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Aspartame and sucralose may cause individual reactions such as headaches in sensitive persons.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acidic components can contribute to tooth enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Excessive intake may lead to insomnia, increased heart rate, and anxiety.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some flavorings may contain trace allergens, e.g., dairy.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled, in moderate amounts. Pairs well with light snacks, sugar‑free desserts, and in mocktails based on non‑alcoholic mixers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.
